catalog_locator: Ch. 5 'Himyar', §5 n, p. 49 (dli.ernet.103575; cross-references ch. 10 'Hijaz: the vowels', §10 m-p, pp. 102-105; the two p. 104 sentences quoted (§10 n and the opening sentence of §10 p, which sits at the foot of p. 104) are on the render (p. 49 n), 5574-5601 (pp. 102-103 m), 5647-5665 (p. 104 n), 5706-5711 (p. 104-105 p)
catalog_quote: We get a more instructive indication in the term muʿaqqad 'halting' with which Hamdānī describes both Himyaritic itself and the dialects influenced by it. It seems that he means the same when he says that the people of Sarw Ḥimyar 'drawl' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim). 'Drawling' in general is due to the absence of stress accent, and was probably a feature of West-Arabian altogether (cf. § 10 p). But South-Arabian must have had a drawling of a much more pronounced character, which produced the two-peak syllables of Minaean and other dialects (cf. Rhodokanakis, Studien, i, 12–56). It is this feature which was so noticeable about Himyaritic even to a Yemenite like Hamdānī. ... [p. 104] This particular staccato quality seems to have been alien to the 'Himyaritic' speech of ancient times, which is on the contrary described as 'halting' (muʿaqqad), we should say 'drawling'. ... [p. 104, §10 p] It seems thus pretty well established that West-Arabian did not possess an expiratory stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rabin infers from al-Hamdānī's tenth-century characterisation of Himyaritic speech as 'halting' (muʿaqqad) and 'drawling' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim) that Himyaritic, like West-Arabian generally, lacked an expiratory (stress) accent, and that its drawl was even more marked than in West-Arabian (compared to the 'two-peak syllables' Rhodokanakis posited for Minaean). No stress position is or can be stated; the claim is an interpretation of medieval impressionistic remarks, not a description from speakers or texts. Supporting passage p. 104: 'This particular staccato quality seems to have been alien to the Himyaritic speech of ancient times, which is on the contrary described as halting (muʿaqqad), we should say drawling.'
new_statements.exceptions: None; Rabin flags that 'drawl'/'staccato' are 'merely impressionist terms' on ground 'not satisfactorily investigated by modern phonetics' (p. 103).
new_statements.domain_note: Not a word-level rule at all: an impression of connected speech reported by Arab philologists (al-Hamdānī, Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab pp. 134-136 ed. Müller) and interpreted by Rabin as absence of stress accent. The only stress-related statement that exists for this languoid; treat as low-confidence and inferential.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog's opaque label "South-Arabian-Unknown-k" is Himyaritic: the languoid's md.ini (saved as glottolog_sout2466_md.ini) carries hhbib altnames "Himyarite, Himyaritic", trigger language code "himyaritic", and its only three references are the Himyaritic surveys Beeston 1981, Robin 2006/2007 (EALL "Ḥimyaritic") and Stein 2008 (Semitica et Classica). Himyaritic is the speech of the Ḥimyar of highland Yemen, attested by three late rhymed texts (ZI 11, Ja 2353, Qāniya hymn) and by 10th-century remarks of al-Hamdānī and other Arab philologists; Robin treats it as a distinct language, Stein 2008 argues the Himyarites wrote Sabaic and the medieval "Himyaritic" is Arabic with a Sayhadic substrate. Not the same as the Old South Arabian (Sabaic saba1279 etc.) or Modern South Arabian languages. No living speakers; the 'stress' remark found is an inference from medieval impressionistic descriptions, not from data.

sources.note: p. 49 par. n: al-Hamdānī's 'halting' (muʿaqqad) and 'drawl' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim) for Himyaritic are read by Rabin as 'due to the absence of stress accent', a West-Arabian trait, with South Arabian having an even more pronounced drawl ('two-peak syllables of Minaean'); p. 104 par. 10 n: the staccato quality of Ẓafār Arabic 'seems to have been alien to the Himyaritic speech of ancient times, which is on the contrary described as halting (muʿaqqad), we should say drawling'; p. 104-105 par. 10 p: 'West-Arabian did not possess an expiratory stress'. No statement of stress position; everything…

Secondary/tertiary: repeats the 'drawl' remark of al-Hamdānī 'suggested to have been due to the absence of stress in Sayhadic or at least stress as was familiar to Arabic-speakers' and links the 'halting' description to pausal glottalization in modern South Arabian dialects; footnote cites Watson 2018 (OUP chapter), but the wording matches Rabin 1951 p. 49. Used only for its bibliography (Beeston 1981, Rabin 1951, Stein 2008, Robin 2007).
